‘Where are we?’ Kenny Dillingham turns introspective to get ASU football back on track

by Jayce Galvez, Cronkite News
October 23, 2026

TEMPE – Following the Arizona State football team’s most recent loss, a 53-25 blowout at the hands of No. 10 Texas Tech, coach Kenny Dillingham held a nearly four-hour meeting with the Sun Devils coaching staff.

“We just assessed ‘OK, where are we? What are the things we want to get better at in the future?’” Dillingham said. “‘Why are we where we’re at? Are there things we could’ve done better structurally, practice-wise, as we were building this thing?’”

Now in his fourth year at the helm, Dillingham is 3-3 this season and 1-2 in Big-12 play, yet he still believes in the capability of his current roster.

“Do we need to make drastic changes? Absolutely not,” Dillingham said. “We still have half of a season left and we haven’t played our best football.”

For the players, that belief in each other is important when trying to build momentum in the middle of the season.

“Going back to the basics,” senior defensive lineman C.J. Fite said. “Knowing who we are, our culture, our standard and not trying to do anything special."

While Dillingham isn’t publicly laying much blame at his players’ feet, he is looking inward for solutions.

“I am letting our football team down,” he said following a 55-19 home loss to unranked Baylor on Oct. 3.

When he first started as head coach in 2023, Dillingham inherited a broken program, still recovering from the effects of the Herm Edwards era at Arizona State. That season, the Sun Devils went 3-9, tied with the previous season for the most losses in a season in the program’s history.

Dillingham made great progress in a short period of time, turning the Sun Devils into a College Football Playoff team by 2024.

“The program had nothing to play for because of a self-imposed bowl ban that followed coach Herm Edwards' tenure, which was being investigated by the NCAA because of allegations of repeated recruiting violations,” ESPN writer Paolo Uggetti said in 2024. “The Sun Devils brought in 23 players in the transfer portal (in Dillingham’s first) season (only one of them was a four-star recruit). 

“Seventeen of them started in the Big 12 title game.”

Dillingham’s tenure at Arizona State is highlighted by winning the Big 12 championship and the College Football Playoff appearance in 2024. That season, the Sun Devils were projected to finish last in the conference. 

“To truly understand the magnitude of what Dillingham is doing in Tempe, one must first appreciate the idiot-shaped crater left by the Sun Devils’ previous leadership,” college football and Washington Post writer Steven Godfrey said at the time. 

But the Sun Devils haven’t been able to sustain that momentum. They went 8-5 last season, losing in the Sun Bowl to Duke, and they aren’t even on that pace this season.

Much like the 2024 season, the Sun Devils are hoping to gain momentum with a win against Kansas State on Saturday at Mountain America Stadium.

“I remember we played a good team that year,” Fite said of a 24-14 win at No. 16 Kansas State. “I think after that game, that’s when we really started rolling.”

A notable roster change at quarterback could help steer the ship. Arizona native and Chandler High School alumnus Mikey Keene will get his first start as a Sun Devil against Kansas State.

Keene replaced Cutter Boley at halftime last Saturday when the Red Raiders led 43-10, the largest halftime deficit the Sun Devils have faced since playing No. 2 Oregon at home in 2012 (43-7).

“I thought Mikey came out and did pretty good for being on the bench for five-and-a-half games,” wide receiver Reed Harris said. “He handled the challenge well.”

Following Saturday's game, Arizona State still has to play two more ranked opponents on the road: No. 2 BYU on Oct. 31 and rival No. 25 Arizona on Nov. 28. The Sun Devils also host Oklahoma State on Nov. 21. The Cowboys are first among other teams receiving votes in the AP poll.

Dillingham is already 1-2 against Arizona. A third loss would be detrimental to the program and a fan base that often measures wins against the Wildcats as a mark of success. 

While offensive issues led to the QB change, the Sun Devils also rank No. 120 in scoring defense out of 138 teams, allowing an average of 32 points per game. It’s a turn of events that few saw coming.

With the success of the 2024 season, fans and analysts believed Arizona State would be a Big-12 contender for years to come, but the Sun Devils haven’t come close to matching the success of that one season, a trend that has plagued previous ASU coaches. 

“The landscape is changing constantly,” Dillingham said. “The strategy of two years ago may be a horrible strategy right now.” 

The Sun Devils have faced highs and lows in Dillingham’s short tenure. How they respond to this latest low may determine the future of the program. 

It’s worth noting that while Dillingham is an ASU alumnus and is widely considered to be as strong a promoter of the program as any coach in the past half century, no football coach has lasted more than six seasons at ASU since the turn of the millennium, and only one (Bruce Snyder) has done so since 1980.
